Q: Android Studio Kotlin: SourceSet with name 'main' not found A:

Solution :

Adding a New Module to Run Kotlin Code in an Android Project

1. Create a New Module

  • Right-click on the app folder in the left panel

  • Select New > Module

  • In the window that opens, select Java or Kotlin Library

  • Library name: playground (or any name you prefer)

  • Class name: Main (or leave it empty)

  • Click Finish

2. Create a Kotlin File

  • Right-click on the src/main/java/... folder inside the newly created playground module

  • Select New > Kotlin Class/File

  • Choose File, give it any name you want (e.g. Test)

3. Write Your Code and Run It

kotlin

fun main() {
    test(1345).....
}

Q: How to convert ISO timestamp to Milliseconds? A:

To convert ISO timestamp to milliseconds you can use the following solution:

Java:

import java.time.Instant;

String isoString = "2026-06-25T12:00:00Z";
long milliseconds = Instant.parse(isoString).toEpochMilli();
System.out.println("ISO timestamp of "+isoString+" is: "+milliseconds+" milliseconds");

Output:

ISO timestamp of 2026-06-25T12:00:00Z is: 1782388800000 milliseconds

Python: you can use datetime.fromisoformat() and multiply the timestamp by 1000 to get the milliseconds as follows:

from datetime import datetime

iso_string = "2026-06-25T12:00:00+00:00"
dt = datetime.fromisoformat(iso_string)
milliseconds = int(dt.timestamp() * 1000)
print(f"ISO timestamp of {iso_string} is: {milliseconds} milliseconds")

Output:

ISO timestamp of 2026-06-25T12:00:00+00:00 is: 1782388800000 milliseconds

Q: == vs is in PyCharm A:

The language runtime "Python" is the same, and that does not depend of what tool you are using to run the Python code.

What may change across different conditions of running Python itself - including version, build, architecture - and then yes, it may be that each of your tools is running a different Python runtime - or at least running Python with different options. In your case, it may even be the same runtime, but idle is in interactive mode, and in pycharm you are running a script.

That said, in Python, the language, regardless of where you are running, the correct way of comparing numbers is withe the == operator. The same number will always equal itself.

What changes is levels of internal optimization of the language: Python is allowed to, in its internal mechanisms, when it perceives it is creating an identical number to one that is already created in the current process, to instead just reuse a reference of the same number. When it does so, it will return "True" if both references are compared with the is operator. That is TOTALLY part of an internal, opaque, optimization, and must not be relied on for any purposes.

So, let me re-state that so it is clear: Python doesn't use direct "CPU numbers˜ when you create integers - just like everything else in the language, integers are objects. When Python creates an object, it reserves an area in memory for it, fills in a data structure including the number of references, its class, and, in the case of numbers, its value encoded in a specific way. Say that when you do orange=500 it puts that at memory address 1000. Memory addresses values themselves are mostly irrelevant in modern computer architectures (because there are a lot, really a lot, of indirections before the data lands in an actual RAM chip, flipping bits, etc), and doubly so in Python - but if they are the same in the same running process, then you are talking about the same object. The Python id(...) function will return the memory address of an object, in cPython) . But getting back to our history: when Python interprets the statement apples=500 in another line of code, depending on the version, optimizations, and most likely the running mode (interactive or programatic), it may find easily that there already is an 500 integer instance created: in that case it binds apples to the same address in memory and it is the same as the previous oranges, or, the optmizations don't detect that, and it will simply create ANOTHER intance of the 500 integer, in another memory position (say, "1200" instead of "1000"): in that case, they will not be the same, as compared with "is", but still completely equivalent, as compared with ==.

Just to illustrate a 3rd time, here is a paste from my terminal - the same Python command - invoked directly, first instructed to run the contents of a string a Python program (non interactive mode), and second, in the interactive mode:

jsbueno@fedora:~$ python -c "orange=500; apple=500; print(orange is apple)"
True
jsbueno@fedora:~$ python
Python 3.14.5 (main, May 11 2026, 00:00:00) [GCC 16.1.1 20260501 (Red Hat 16.1.1-1)] on linux
Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information.
>>> orange = 500
>>> apple = 500
>>> orange is apple
False
>>>

See? In this case, the compiler piece (part of the runtime) takes some code where the number "500" shows up twice in the same chunk, so it is smart enough to just create one. In the interactive mode, each time I press <enter>, the compiler piece is invoked just for that line of code: so when I declare "apple = 500" it is "cheaper" for it just to create another, instead of looking around to see if a previous "500" would already exist.

Q: How do I code without being completely dependent on AI? A:

In many ways, AI is the "Easy Button" — press it and the problem goes away. Sort of.

after a threshold I just use AI to not stay behind while the world instantly generates code using AI.

You aren't competing with classmates in school; you are competing against yourself. Forget what others are doing. Education is supposed to be about training and moulding your brain, fine-tuning your thought processes, and expanding your mind; it's not about comparing yourself to others. In many ways, education is very inward-focused.

Coding without being dependent on AI will need to be an intentional decision. Don't push the "Easy Button". Seek out official documentation, forum posts, etc. When search engines thrust their AI slop in your face, just know to scroll down the page by one or two mouse wheels or a couple of thumb flicks if you are on your mobile. It becomes muscle memory pretty quickly.

Now for a bit of a frame-challenge: it's OK to use AI while you are learning. It can give you access to concepts and buzzwords that you can follow up with additional searches for original source material. Rather than "push the Easy Button and make the problem go away", use AI to help fine-tune your search, and identify adjacent topics that allow you to dive even deeper.

Here's what you want to avoid: offloading your thought processes to AI.

You be the one to think, not AI.
